sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Haumiatiketike** ​(*haumiatiketike*) ‌— Wild ‌Food, ​Fernroot ​· Haumia ​tied ​to ​the earth ‌— ​belongs ​to the ‌Polynesian ​tradition, ‌where it ​is ‌catalogued ​under the ​domain ​"Wild ​Food, Fernroot". ​The ‌name ​means "Haumia ‌tied ​to ‌the earth".

​**Haumiatiketike** ‌is ​wild food, ‌fernroot. ​The ​name means ‌"Haumia ‌tied ‌to the ​earth" ​and ‌belongs to ​the ​polynesian ‌tradition.

PuniCodex ​restores ​the ‌name as ​**Haumiatiketike** ‌and ​serves its ​temple ​at ​[its temple](https://punicodex.com/haumiatiketike/). ‌The ‌restoration ​needs no ‌distinctive ​letters ​or diacritics ‌its ‌ASCII ‌form would ‌lose, ​which ‌places the ​name ​in ​Tier 2. ‌The ​plain ​ASCII form ​*haumiatiketike* ‌survives ​as a ​modern ​convenience ‌imposed by ​the ‌early ​domain-name system; ‌the ​restoration, ‌not the ‌fallback, ​is ​the form ​the ​project ‌defends as ‌philologically ​complete.

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
The ​name is ‌attested in ‌modern Polynesian ​orthographies; macron ​usage follows ​each tradition’s ​reference dictionaries. ​Etymologically the ‌name means ​"Haumia tied ​to the ‌earth".

The ​ASCII form ‌*haumiatiketike* survives ​only because ‌the early ​domain-name system ​could not ​carry diacritics; ​it is ​a technological ‌compromise, not ​an ancient ‌spelling. The ​Unicode restoration ‌**Haumiatiketike** recovers ​the full ‌diacritic detail ​of the ‌scholarly transliteration ​directly in ​the address ‌bar. The ‌restoration needs ‌no distinctive ​letters or ​diacritics its ‌ASCII form ​would lose, ​which places ‌the name ​in Tier ​2.

The ‌letter-by-letter ​transformation runs:

‌- **h** ​→ **H** ​— Same, ​capitalized
- ​**a** → ‌**a** — ‌Same
- ​**u** → ‌**u** — ​Same
- ​**m** → ‌**m** — ‌Same
- ‌**i** → ‌**i** — ​Same
- ‌**a** → ​**a** — ​Same

sections.body:
The ​reconstructed ‌pronunciation of ‌the ​name ​is ​**/haumiatiketike/** — ​Restored ​scholarly ‌form.

​Phoneme by ​phoneme:

‌- ​**haumiatiketike** ‌— ​The canonical ‌restored ​form ​Haumiatiketike.

​For the ​modern ​speaker, ‌the ​closest approximation ‌is: ​Say ‌"haumiatiketike" ​with the ‌stress ​and ‌length ​implied by ​the ‌scholarly ‌restoration ‌"Haumiatiketike".

​The ASCII ​form ‌"haumiatiketike" ​is ​a DNS ‌compromise; ​the ​restoration ‌"Haumiatiketike" preserves ​the ‌name's ​scholarly ​dignity.

The ​pronunciation ​given ‌above ‌reconstructs the ​sound ‌world ​in ​which ‌Haumiatiketike was ‌invoked. ‌Modern ‌speakers ​should not ‌expect ​exact ​identity ​with ancient ‌phonology; ​the ​reconstruction ​is a ‌scholarly ​compass, ​not ​a performance ‌prescription. ​The ‌restoration ​Haumiatiketike ‌keeps the ​prosodic ‌information ‌visible ​even when ​the ​name ​is ‌typed in ‌plain ​ASCII.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
The ​stories of ‌Haumiatiketike ‌place ​wild food, ​fernroot ​at the ​center ​of a ‌living ​mythological ​world.

### ‌Origins ​(Myth)

Haumiatiketike ‌appears ​in polynesian ‌tradition ​as ​wild food, ​fernroot. ​The name's ​meaning, ‌"Haumia ​tied to ‌the ​earth", shapes ‌the ​narratives told ‌about ​this ‌figure.

### ​Worship ​and Memory ‌(Cult)

‌Devotees and ‌later ​tradition-keepers ​preserved Haumiatiketike ‌in ​ritual, text, ​and ‌iconography, ​ensuring the ​name ‌survived into ​the ‌modern scholarly ​record.

​The ​myths of ​Haumiatiketike ‌survive in ‌fragments, ​summaries, ‌and later ​retellings. ​Each version ‌reflects ‌the interests ‌of ‌its ​tellers — ‌poets, ​priests, philosophers, ​and ​scholars. The ‌PuniCodex ​entry ​does not ​privilege ‌a single ​version; ​it ​gathers the ‌attestations ​so that ‌readers ​can compare ‌them. ​The ‌restoration Haumiatiketike ‌gives ​the figure ​a ​stable name ​around ‌which ‌these variants ​orbit.

sections.label: Archaeology & Material Evidence
sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body:
No ​monument, ‌inscription, ‌or artifact ​in ​the ​current ​PuniCodex ​corpus ‌is ​yet assigned ​to ‌Haumiatiketike ​with ‌certainty. ​That ‌absence ​should be ​read ​honestly: ​for ​a ‌Polynesian ​name ‌of this ​type ‌the ​material ‌record ​is ‌expected to ​be ​thin, ‌and ‌the ‌primary ​evidence ​remains the ‌textual ​testimony ​gathered ‌in ​the ​Scholarly ‌Sources section.

​Were ‌such ​evidence ​to ​surface, ​it ‌would take ‌recognizable ​forms: ‌votive ​or ​dedicatory ‌inscriptions ‌naming Haumiatiketike, ‌sanctuary ‌or ​cult ‌remains ​tied ​to wild ​food ‌and ​iconography ​matching ​its ‌traditional ​attributes (name ​and ​domain). ‌Each ​candidate ‌would ​be ‌weighed against ​the ‌reconstructed ‌form ​of ​the ​name ​before entering ‌the ‌scholarly ​record.

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body:
To ​contemplate ‌Haumiatiketike is ‌to ​hold ​the idea ​of ​wild ​Food, ‌Fernroot in ​the ​mind ‌and to ​ask ‌what ​of ‌it endures. ​The ​name ​means "Haumia ​tied ​to ‌the ​earth" — ‌and ​a ‌name that ​carries ‌its ​meaning ‌so openly ​invites ​meditation ‌rather than ‌mere ‌recollection. ​The ​tradition remembers ‌the ​name ​as wild ‌Food, ​Fernroot ​· ‌Haumia tied ​to ‌the ​earth.

​Sit with ​the ​restored ‌form — ‌Haumiatiketike ​— ‌and ​the diacritics ​themselves ‌become ‌the practice: ‌each ‌mark ​is ‌a small ​act ​of ​attention, a ‌refusal ​to ​let ​the plain ‌ASCII ​form ​*haumiatiketike* stand ​in ‌for ​the ‌whole. What ​the ‌tradition ​preserved in ‌this ‌name, ​the ​restoration asks ​the ​reader ‌to preserve ‌in ​turn.
